focus: Exodus 17 records two events at Rephidim that answer the people’s question, “Is the LORD among us or not?” (Exodus 17:7). The LORD gives water from the rock when Israel quarrels with Moses and tests Him, and He gives victory when Amalek attacks, which Moses commemorates with an altar named The-LORD-Is-My-Banner.

sections.title: Water from the Rock at Massah and Meribah
sections.summary: At Rephidim there is no water, and the people contend with Moses until he cries out that they are almost ready to stone him. The LORD stands before Moses on the rock in Horeb and Moses strikes it, and water comes out, but the place is named Massah and Meribah because the people tempted the LORD, saying, “Is the LORD among us or not?” (Exodus 17:7).

sections.title: Israel Prevails over Amalek While Moses’ Hands Are Held Up
sections.summary: When Amalek attacks, Joshua leads the fight while Moses stands on the hill with the rod of God, and Israel prevails whenever Moses holds up his hand. As Moses’ hands grow heavy, Aaron and Hur hold them steady until sunset, and Joshua defeats Amalek.

sections.title: A Memorial Written and an Altar Named The-LORD-Is-My-Banner
sections.summary: The LORD tells Moses, “Write this for a memorial in the book” (Exodus 17:14), declaring that He will blot out the remembrance of Amalek. Moses builds an altar and names it The-LORD-Is-My-Banner, for the LORD will have war with Amalek from generation to generation.

1.brief: The congregation travels from the Wilderness of Sin by the LORD’s command and camps at Rephidim, but there is no water to drink. Israel arrives where God led them and finds a new and real need.
1.explain:
“Then all the congregation of the children of Israel set out on their journey from the Wilderness of Sin, according to the commandment of the LORD,”

Israel moves on from the place where God gave the manna. They travel “according to the commandment of the LORD,” literally according to the mouth of the LORD. They are going where God leads them, probably by the movement of the cloud (13:21–22).

“and camped in Rephidim; but there was no water for the people to drink.”

They camp at “Rephidim,” and there is “no water.” The need is real. In the desert, a large company with children and animals could not survive long without water. Israel arrives where God led them and finds a new need.
1.notes: Numbers 33:12–14 lists two stops, Dophkah and Alush, between the Wilderness of Sin and Rephidim. The location of Rephidim is uncertain. It is often placed in the southwestern Sinai Peninsula, near the approach to Mount Sinai.

2.brief: The people contend with Moses and demand water, and Moses asks, “Why do you contend with me? Why do you tempt the LORD?” Their quarrel with Moses is really a testing of God.
2.explain:
“Therefore the people contended with Moses, and said, ‘Give us water, that we may drink.”

The people “contended with Moses.” The word describes a quarrel or a legal dispute. They do not ask God for water. They demand it from Moses: “Give us water.”

“So Moses said to them, ‘Why do you contend with me? Why do you tempt the LORD?”

Moses answers with two questions. Their quarrel with him is really a quarrel with God. To “tempt the LORD” means to put Him to the test, demanding that He prove Himself. Their quarrel with Moses is really a testing of God.
2.notes: The Hebrew verb translated “tempt” here means to test or try. Deuteronomy 6:16 warns, “You shall not tempt the LORD your God as you tempted Him in Massah.” Jesus quoted that verse when the devil tempted Him (Matthew 4:7).

3.brief: The thirsty people complain against Moses and ask why he brought them out of Egypt to kill them, their children, and their livestock with thirst. Their real distress turns into accusation.
3.explain:
“And the people thirsted there for water, and the people complained against Moses,”

The thirst was real, and “the people thirsted.” But instead of crying out to God, they “complained against Moses.”

“and said, ‘Why is it you have brought us up out of Egypt, to kill us and our children and our livestock with thirst?”

They accuse Moses of bringing them out “to kill us.” Their fear for their “children” and “livestock” is understandable, but the accusation is not. God had given water at Marah and bread in the wilderness. Their real distress turns into accusation against the one God sent.

4.brief: Moses cries out to the LORD, “What shall I do with this people? They are almost ready to stone me!” Moses takes the crisis to God as the people turn against him.
4.explain:
“So Moses cried out to the LORD, saying, ‘What shall I do with this people?”

Moses does what the people failed to do. He “cried out to the LORD.” He brings the crisis to God and asks what to do.

“They are almost ready to stone me!”

The situation has become dangerous. The people are close to stoning Moses. Moses takes the crisis to God as the people turn against him.

5.brief: The LORD tells Moses to go ahead of the people with some of the elders and take the rod with which he struck the river. The rod of judgment on Egypt will now be used to provide for Israel.
5.explain:
“And the LORD said to Moses, ‘Go on before the people, and take with you some of the elders of Israel.”

God tells Moses to go ahead of the people with “some of the elders.” The elders will be witnesses to what God does.

“Also take in your hand your rod with which you struck the river, and go.”

Moses is to take “your rod with which you struck the river.” That rod had turned the Nile to blood (7:20). The rod of judgment on Egypt will now be used to provide for Israel.

6.brief: The LORD says, “I will stand before you there on the rock in Horeb,” and when Moses strikes the rock, water comes out for the people, and Moses does so before the elders. God’s presence at the rock brings water, and 1 Corinthians 10:4 later says that Rock was Christ.
6.explain:
“Behold, I will stand before you there on the rock in Horeb;”

God promises His presence: “I will stand before you there on the rock.” The people asked whether the LORD was among them (17:7). God answers by standing at the very place where He will give water. “Horeb” is another name for Sinai, the mountain of God (3:1).

“and you shall strike the rock, and water will come out of it, that the people may drink.”

Moses is to “strike the rock.” Water will come from it, enough for the whole people. God provides from the most unlikely source, solid rock in a dry land. Paul later writes that Israel “drank of that spiritual Rock that followed them, and that Rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:4). The water was real provision for real thirst, and Paul teaches that Christ was the true source of Israel’s provision in the wilderness. Many Christians have also seen in the struck rock a picture of Christ, struck for His people and giving living water (John 7:37–39). That picture is a devotional reading, distinct from Paul’s own statement.

“And Moses did so in the sight of the elders of Israel.”

Moses obeys with the elders watching. They witnessed that the water came from God.
6.notes: Psalm 78:15–16 and Psalm 105:41 recall the water from the rock among God’s great works.

7.brief: Moses names the place Massah and Meribah because Israel quarreled and tested the LORD, saying, “Is the LORD among us or not?” The names preserve the memory of the people doubting the God who had just provided for them.
7.explain:
“So he called the name of the place Massah and Meribah,”

Moses names the place twice. “Massah” means testing, and “Meribah” means quarreling.

“because of the contention of the children of Israel, and because they tempted the LORD,”

The names record what the people did. They quarreled with Moses, and they put the LORD to the test.

“saying, ‘Is the LORD among us or not?”

The narrator gives the heart of their testing: “Is the LORD among us or not?” The question doubts God’s presence. They had seen the plagues, the sea, the manna, and the pillar of cloud. Still they doubted. The names preserve the memory of the people doubting the God who had just provided for them.
7.notes:
Psalm 95:8–9 warns, “Do not harden your hearts, as in the rebellion,” recalling the day the fathers tested God in the wilderness.

A similar event occurred near the end of the wilderness period, also named Meribah (Numbers 20:1–13). There God told Moses to speak to the rock. Moses spoke rashly, called the people rebels, and struck the rock twice. God said that Moses and Aaron did not believe Him or honor Him as holy before Israel (Numbers 20:12; Psalm 106:32–33).

8.brief: Amalek comes and fights with Israel at Rephidim. A new threat arises from outside the camp.
8.explain:
“Now Amalek came and fought with Israel in Rephidim.”

A new threat comes from outside. “Amalek,” a desert people descended from Esau (Genesis 36:12), attacks Israel at Rephidim. Deuteronomy 25:17–18 adds that Amalek attacked the weak and weary stragglers at the rear of Israel’s column.
8.notes: Deuteronomy 25:18 says of Amalek that “he did not fear God.” This helps explain the severity of God’s judgment on Amalek in 17:14–16.

9.brief: Moses tells Joshua to choose men and fight Amalek, while he will stand on the hilltop “with the rod of God in my hand.” Joshua leads the battle below while Moses holds the sign of God’s power above.
9.explain:
“And Moses said to Joshua, ‘Choose us some men and go out, fight with Amalek.”

“Joshua” appears here for the first time in Scripture. Moses gives him the task of choosing fighting men and leading the battle. Israel has no trained army, but they must defend themselves.

“Tomorrow I will stand on the top of the hill with the rod of God in my hand.”

Moses will take his place on the hill “with the rod of God in my hand.” The rod is called “the rod of God” (4:20) because it is the sign of God’s power. Joshua leads the battle below while Moses holds the sign of God’s power above.
9.notes: Joshua’s name was originally Hoshea (Numbers 13:16). Moses changed it to Joshua, meaning the LORD is salvation. The Greek form of the name is Jesus.

10.brief: Joshua does as Moses said and fights Amalek, and Moses, Aaron, and Hur go up to the top of the hill. The battle and the hilltop scene happen together.
10.explain:
“So Joshua did as Moses said to him, and fought with Amalek.”

Joshua obeys Moses and leads the fight.

“And Moses, Aaron, and Hur went up to the top of the hill.”

Moses goes up with “Aaron” and “Hur.” This is the first mention of Hur. He appears again with Aaron as a leader during Moses’ absence on the mountain (24:14). The battle below and the scene on the hill happen together.
10.notes: Jewish tradition identifies Hur as Miriam’s husband, but Scripture does not say so. A Hur of the tribe of Judah was grandfather of Bezalel, the tabernacle craftsman (31:2; 1 Chronicles 2:19–20). Whether he is the same man is uncertain.

11.brief: Whenever Moses holds up his hand, Israel prevails, and whenever he lets it down, Amalek prevails. The outcome of the battle depends on what happens on the hill, showing that victory comes from God.
11.explain:
“And so it was, when Moses held up his hand, that Israel prevailed;”

When Moses “held up his hand,” Israel “prevailed.” The battle is tied to what happens on the hill.

“and when he let down his hand, Amalek prevailed.”

When Moses’ hand dropped, Amalek gained the upper hand. The outcome of the battle depends on what happens on the hill, showing that victory comes from God. The text does not explain whether the raised hand was prayer, a signal, or a lifting up of the rod of God. Many interpreters understand it as a picture of dependence on God and intercession.

12.brief: When Moses’ hands grow heavy, Aaron and Hur seat him on a stone and hold up his hands on either side, so that they stay steady until sunset. Moses’ strength fails, but others help bear his burden.
12.explain:
“But Moses’ hands became heavy;”

Moses grows tired. His “hands became heavy.” Even God’s chosen leader has limits.

“so they took a stone and put it under him, and he sat on it.”

Aaron and Hur give Moses a stone to sit on.

“And Aaron and Hur supported his hands, one on one side, and the other on the other side;”

They hold up his hands, one on each side. Moses could not do it alone. Others help bear his burden.

“and his hands were steady until the going down of the sun.”

With their help, Moses’ hands stayed “steady,” firm and unwavering, until sunset. The word steady is related to the Hebrew word for faithfulness.

13.brief: Joshua defeats Amalek and his people with the edge of the sword. The battle ends in Israel’s victory.
13.explain:
“So Joshua defeated Amalek and his people with the edge of the sword.”

Joshua “defeated Amalek.” The phrase “with the edge of the sword” means in battle. Joshua fought, Moses held up his hands, and Aaron and Hur supported him. The victory came through the shared action of God’s people, and the next verses credit it to the LORD.

14.brief: The LORD tells Moses, “Write this for a memorial in the book,” to be recounted to Joshua, for He will utterly blot out the remembrance of Amalek. God wants this victory and His judgment on Amalek remembered.
14.explain:
“Then the LORD said to Moses, ‘Write this for a memorial in the book”

God commands Moses to “write this.” This is the first mention in Scripture of Moses writing. The record is to be a “memorial,” a lasting reminder.

“and recount it in the hearing of Joshua,”

Moses is to tell it to “Joshua.” Joshua would lead Israel into Canaan, and he needed to remember God’s word about Amalek.

“that I will utterly blot out the remembrance of Amalek from under heaven.”

Amalek’s very memory is to be erased. God wants this victory and His judgment on Amalek remembered.
14.notes: Deuteronomy 25:17–19 repeats this command. Saul was later told to destroy Amalek and failed to obey fully (1 Samuel 15:2–3, 9). David also fought the Amalekites (1 Samuel 30), and a remnant was destroyed in Hezekiah’s time (1 Chronicles 4:42–43).

15.brief: Moses builds an altar and names it The-LORD-Is-My-Banner. The name credits the victory to the LORD, who led Israel in the battle.
15.explain:
“And Moses built an altar and called its name, The-LORD-Is-My-Banner;”

Moses builds “an altar” to mark the victory. He names it “The-LORD-Is-My-Banner.” A banner was a standard or flag raised on a pole, around which an army rallied. Moses held up the rod of God on the hill. Now he declares that the LORD Himself is the banner under which Israel fights. The name credits the victory to the LORD.
15.notes: The Hebrew name is often transliterated Yahweh Nissi. The word for banner is also used in Isaiah 11:10, where the Root of Jesse will stand as a banner to the peoples.

16.brief: Moses says that the LORD has sworn to have war with Amalek “from generation to generation.” The conflict with Amalek will continue beyond this day.
16.explain:
“for he said, ‘Because the LORD has sworn:”

Moses explains the altar’s name with God’s oath. The Hebrew here is difficult. It may read a hand upon the throne of the LORD, referring to an oath, or a hand upon the banner of the LORD.

“the LORD will have war with Amalek from generation to generation.”

The conflict with Amalek will continue beyond this day.
16.notes: The Hebrew of the first part of this verse is uncertain. The Hebrew text has a word meaning “throne” (kes). Some interpreters propose reading instead the Hebrew word for “banner” (nes), a different word, which would connect the line with the altar’s name in 17:15. That is a proposed reading, not the wording of the Hebrew text. The NKJV takes the line as an oath.
